title: Rise, Rama: The Dawn Has Come
hookLine: a sage wakes two princes by a river in the dark. temples still sing his words to wake God every dawn
carry: the day begins with the sacred
tomorrow: a boy asks Death what comes after. why does Death draw him a chariot?

lines: TWO PRINCES ON A BED OF GRASS.
RISE, RAMA. THE DAWN HAS COME.
cards: Two young princes are asleep on a bed of grass beside a river, a long way from the palace. Rama and his brother Lakshmana have left home with the sage Vishvamitra, and this is their first night out.
In the Ramayana, as the night ends, the sage leans over the sleeping boys and wakes them with a verse. Rama, blessed son of Kausalya, the eastern twilight is beginning. Get up, tiger among men.
The day's rites to the gods are waiting.

teach.b: The boys get up, bathe, say their morning prayers, bow to their teacher, and walk on. It's a small scene in a long epic.
But those two lines became the opening of the Venkateshwara Suprabhatam, the hymn sung before dawn at the great temple at Tirumala to wake the Lord, and played at sunrise in many Hindu homes.
The words a sage used to wake a prince are used to wake God, and the household wakes with him.

teach.h: THE DAY BEGINS WITH THE SACRED.
teach.b: That's the teaching: in Hindu life, the day begins with the sacred. The time just before sunrise even has a name, brahma muhurta, prized for prayer, study and meditation.

Ayurveda's Ashtanga Hridaya opens its daily routine right there: a healthy person should rise in brahma muhurta, to protect their life. And many families keep a tiny prayer for the very first waking moment.
You look at your open palms and say: at the tips of the hands lives Lakshmi, in the middle Sarasvati, at the base Govinda; so at dawn, look at your hands.
Wealth, learning and God, in the hands you're about to use all day. Now think where most hands go first: to a glowing screen, and the day arrives from somewhere else.
Vishvamitra's verse and the palm prayer turn that around. Not everyone can rise in the dark, a new parent, a night-shift worker, someone who's sick; the verse speaks to the healthy.

teach.h: THE FIRST MINUTE, BEFORE THE PHONE.
teach.b: But anyone can give the first minute to something holy before the phone gets it.

how: Many Hindus rise in brahma muhurta for prayer, look at their palms on waking and say 'karagre vasate Lakshmi', or play the Venkateshwara Suprabhatam, which opens with Vishvamitra's words to Rama and is sung before dawn at Tirumala; Ayurvedic texts also recommend waking then for a person in health.

games.why: Vishvamitra woke Rama for the morning rites, and families still begin by looking at their palms: Lakshmi, Sarasvati, Govinda.

practice: Try the palm prayer now, the way many families do on waking. Open your hands and look at them: fingertips, palms, the base of the palm.

If you pray, say the verse, karagre vasate Lakshmi, or just its meaning: Lakshmi, Sarasvati, Govinda, in these hands. If you don't, look anyway and ask what these hands will do today. Tomorrow, try looking at them before the phone.

wordCard.voice: The daily routine. In the Ashtanga Hridaya it begins in brahma muhurta, before sunrise; in many Hindu homes it begins with the palms, or a suprabhatam, before anything else.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the time before sunrise, set apart in Hindu tradition for waking, prayer and study.

carryVoice: Your line: the day begins with the sacred. Your hands first, then the phone. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 23.1–4 (Vishvamitra wakes Rama and Lakshmana on their bed of grass at dawn; they bathe, pray and greet him)
